A note on some upper bounds for the Frobenius norm of the qq-deformed commutator

Motoyuki NOBORI Address: Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Ehime University, 2-5 Bunkyo-cho, Matsuyama 790-8577, Japan Email: m819002c@mails.cc.ehime-u.ac.jp
Abstract

For two square complex matrices A,B,A,B, and a real number qq, the qq-deformed commutator of AA and BB is defined as A​B−q​B​AAB-qBA. We give some upper bounds on the Frobenius norm of the qq-deformed commutator in the case q≥0q\geq 0. All of the inequalities derived in this paper generalize the Böttcher-Wenzel inequality.

Keywords: 
Böttcher-Wenzel inequality, qq-deformed commutator, Ky Fan (2,2)-norm (15A45, 15A60)

1 Introduction

We write Mm,n​(ℂ)M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}) for the vector space of all m×nm\times n complex matrices with the inner product ⟨A,B⟩=tr⁡(A​B∗)\langle A,B\rangle=\mathrm{tr}(AB^{*}), where B∗=BT¯B^{*}=\overline{B^{T}} is the conjugate transpose of BB and tr\mathrm{tr} denotes the trace. The Böttcher-Wenzel inequality gives the following upper bound on the Frobenius norm of the commutator of two square matrices AA and BB:

‖A​B−B​A‖F2≤2​‖A‖F2​‖B‖F2,\displaystyle\|AB-BA\|_{F}^{2}\leq 2\|A\|_{F}^{2}\|B\|_{F}^{2}, (1)

where ‖A‖F=⟨A,A⟩\|A\|_{F}=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle} is the Frobenius norm. Inequality (1) was conjectured to hold for all square real matrices AA and BB in 2005 [3]. After some proofs in the general case (cf. [12] for the real case and [1, 4] for the complex case), several subsequent problems have been considered (cf. [6, 9]). For example, as an inequality whose upper bound is tighter than that of (1),

‖A​B−B​A‖F2≤2​‖A‖(2),22​‖B‖F2\displaystyle\|AB-BA\|_{F}^{2}\leq 2\|A\|_{(2),2}^{2}\|B\|_{F}^{2} (2)

holds [1], where ‖A‖(2),2=σ12​(A)+σ22​(A)\|A\|_{(2),2}=\sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}(A)+\sigma_{2}^{2}(A)} is the Ky Fan (2,2)-norm, and σ1​(A)≥⋯≥σn​(A)\sigma_{1}(A)\geq\dots\geq\sigma_{n}(A) are its singular values. A characterization of its equality case is given in [5]. Some generalizations of (1) by changing commutators and norms have also been investigated (cf. [11, 10, 7]). Especially in [7], sharp upper bounds on the Frobenius norm of the qq-deformed commutator defined as A​B−q​B​AAB-qBA for a real number qq and two square complex matrices A,BA,B are analyzed: an inequality for ‖A​B−q​B​A‖F\|AB-qBA\|_{F} is called sharp at q′q^{\prime} if there exist non-zero matrices AA and BB satisfying its equality at the point q=q′q=q^{\prime}. The following results are known [7]:

  1. (i)

    If q≤0q\leq 0, then the sharp bound is given by

    ‖A​B−q​B​A‖F2≤(1−q)2​‖A‖F2​‖B‖F2.\displaystyle\|AB-qBA\|_{F}^{2}\leq(1-q)^{2}\|A\|_{F}^{2}\|B\|_{F}^{2}.
  2. (ii)

    If q>0q>0 and AA or BB is normal, then the sharp bound is given by

    ‖A​B−q​B​A‖F2≤(1+q2)​‖A‖F2​‖B‖F2.\displaystyle\|AB-qBA\|_{F}^{2}\leq(1+q^{2})\|A\|_{F}^{2}\|B\|_{F}^{2}. (3)

    Also, if AA is normal, then

    ‖A​B−q​B​A‖F2≤(1+q2)​‖A‖(2),22​‖B‖F2\displaystyle\|AB-qBA\|_{F}^{2}\leq(1+q^{2})\|A\|_{(2),2}^{2}\|B\|_{F}^{2}

    holds for all complex square matrices BB.

It is also reported in [7] that inequality (3) fails for some q≥0q\geq 0 and non-normal matrices A,BA,B. In this paper, we derive some upper bounds on the Frobenius norm of the qq-deformed commutator in the case q≥0q\geq 0.

Theorem 1.1.

Let nn be a positive integer, A,BA,B be n×nn\times n complex matrices, and q≥0q\geq 0.

  1. (i)

    If q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1], then

    ‖A​B−q​B​A‖F2\displaystyle\|AB-qBA\|_{F}^{2} ≤{(1+q)​‖A‖(2),22−2​q​(1−q)​σn2​(A)}​‖B‖F2.\displaystyle\leq\{(1+q)\|A\|_{(2),2}^{2}-2q(1-q)\sigma_{n}^{2}(A)\}\|B\|_{F}^{2}. (4)
  2. (ii)

    If q∈[1,+∞)q\in[1,+\infty), then

    ‖A​B−q​B​A‖F2\displaystyle\|AB-qBA\|_{F}^{2} ≤{(q2+q)​‖A‖(2),22−2​(q−1)​σn2​(A)}​‖B‖F2.\displaystyle\leq\{(q^{2}+q)\|A\|_{(2),2}^{2}-2(q-1)\sigma_{n}^{2}(A)\}\|B\|_{F}^{2}. (5)

Inequalities (4) and (5) are generalizations of (2), for both sides of these inequalities coincide with those of (2) if q=1q=1. The above inequalities and their equality conditions will be derived in section 2. We also give two other upper bounds on ‖A​B−q​B​A‖F\|AB-qBA\|_{F} that are generalizations of (2), and their equality conditions. Then we see that the upper bounds given in sections 1 and 2 are sharp at some limited points pp. In section 3, we explore the existence of upper bounds on ‖A​B−q​B​A‖F\|AB-qBA\|_{F} tighter than those in Theorem 1.1.

Here, we introduce the additional notation used in this paper. We abbreviate Mn,n​(ℂ)M_{n,n}(\mathbb{C}) and Mn,1​(ℂ)M_{n,1}(\mathbb{C}) to Mn​(ℂ)M_{n}(\mathbb{C}) and ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}, respectively. We denote by InI_{n} the identity matrix of order nn, and we use OnO_{n} to denote the zero matrix of order nn. We write ℝ,ℕ\mathbb{R},\mathbb{N} as the set of real and natural numbers, respectively. If A,B∈Mn​(ℂ)A,B\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C}) are Hermitian, then B≥AB\geq A means that B−AB-A is positive semidefinite.

2 Main results

We first prove Theorem 1.1. Let nn be a positive integer. We call a matrix J∈Mn​(ℂ)J\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C}) a density matrix if JJ satisfies tr⁡(J)=1\mathrm{tr}(J)=1 and J≥OnJ\geq O_{n}. In the proof of Theorem 1.1, proving that

tr⁡(J⁡(A​A∗+A∗​A))−|tr⁡(J​A)|2≤‖A‖(2),22\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}(J(AA^{*}+A^{*}A))-|\mathrm{tr}(JA)|^{2}\leq\|A\|_{(2),2}^{2}

for all matrices A∈Mn​(ℂ)A\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C}) and density matrices J∈Mn​(ℂ)J\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C}) is the most important step. And its argument is guided by the proof of the following statement:

tr⁡(J⁡(A​A∗+A∗​A))−2​|tr⁡(J​A)|2≤‖A‖(2),22\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}(J(AA^{*}+A^{*}A))-2|\mathrm{tr}(JA)|^{2}\leq\|A\|_{(2),2}^{2} (6)

for all matrices A∈Mn​(ℂ)A\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C}) and density matrices J∈Mn​(ℂ)J\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C}) ([1], Theorems 9 and 13).

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Let nn be a positive integer and A,B∈Mn​(ℂ)A,B\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C}). If AA or BB is the zero matrix, then A​B−q​B​A=OnAB-qBA=O_{n} and clearly the inequalities in the theorem hold. Hence, we consider the case where A,B≠OnA,B\neq O_{n}. Let q∈[0,1].q\in[0,1]. Taking the sum of

‖A​B−q​B​A‖F2=tr⁡(A∗​A​B​B∗+q2​A​A∗​B∗​B−q​A​B​A∗​B∗−q​B​A​B∗​A∗)\displaystyle\|AB-qBA\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}(A^{*}ABB^{*}+q^{2}AA^{*}B^{*}B-qABA^{*}B^{*}-qBAB^{*}A^{*})

and

‖A∗​B+q​B​A∗‖F2=tr⁡(A​A∗​B​B∗+q2​A∗​A​B∗​B+q​A​B​A∗​B∗+q​B​A​B∗​A∗)\displaystyle\|A^{*}B+qBA^{*}\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}(AA^{*}BB^{*}+q^{2}A^{*}AB^{*}B+qABA^{*}B^{*}+qBAB^{*}A^{*})

gives

‖A​B−q​B​A‖F2+‖A∗​B+q​B​A∗‖F2=tr⁡((B∗​B+q2​B​B∗)​(A​A∗+A∗​A)).\displaystyle\|AB-qBA\|_{F}^{2}+\|A^{*}B+qBA^{*}\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}((B^{*}B+q^{2}BB^{*})(AA^{*}+A^{*}A)). (7)

From the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

|tr⁡((B​B∗+q​B∗​B)​A∗)|\displaystyle|\mathrm{tr}((BB^{*}+qB^{*}B)A^{*})| =|⟨A∗​B+q​B​A∗,B⟩|\displaystyle=|\langle A^{*}B+qBA^{*},B\rangle|
≤‖A∗​B+q​B​A∗‖F​‖B‖F.\displaystyle\leq\|A^{*}B+qBA^{*}\|_{F}\|B\|_{F}.

It follows from the above inequality and (7) that

‖A​B−q​B​A‖F2\displaystyle\|AB-qBA\|_{F}^{2} =tr⁡((B∗​B+q2​B​B∗)​(A​A∗+A∗​A))−‖A∗​B+q​B​A∗‖F2\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}((B^{*}B+q^{2}BB^{*})(AA^{*}+A^{*}A))-\|A^{*}B+qBA^{*}\|_{F}^{2}
≤tr⁡((B∗​B+q2​B​B∗)​(A​A∗+A∗​A))−|tr⁡((B​B∗+q​B∗​B)​A∗)|2‖B‖F2\displaystyle\begin{split}&\leq\mathrm{tr}((B^{*}B+q^{2}BB^{*})(AA^{*}+A^{*}A))\\ &\quad\quad-\frac{|\mathrm{tr}((BB^{*}+qB^{*}B)A^{*})|^{2}}{\|B\|_{F}^{2}}\end{split} (8)
=(tr⁡((B∗​B+q​B​B∗)​(A​A∗+A∗​A))−|tr⁡((B​B∗+q​B∗​B)​A∗)|2‖B‖F2)\displaystyle=(\mathrm{tr}((B^{*}B+qBB^{*})(AA^{*}+A^{*}A))-\frac{|\mathrm{tr}((BB^{*}+qB^{*}B)A^{*})|^{2}}{\|B\|_{F}^{2}})
−q⁡(1−q)​tr​((A​A∗+A∗​A)​B∗​B)\displaystyle\quad-q(1-q)\mathrm{tr}((AA^{*}+A^{*}A)B^{*}B)
≕k1+k2,\displaystyle\eqcolon k_{1}+k_{2}, (9)

where

k1\displaystyle k_{1} =tr⁡((B∗​B+q​B​B∗)​(A​A∗+A∗​A))−|tr⁡((B​B∗+q​B∗​B)​A∗)|2‖B‖F2,\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}((B^{*}B+qBB^{*})(AA^{*}+A^{*}A))-\frac{|\mathrm{tr}((BB^{*}+qB^{*}B)A^{*})|^{2}}{\|B\|_{F}^{2}},
k2\displaystyle k_{2} =−q⁡(1−q)​tr​((A​A∗+A∗​A)​B∗​B).\displaystyle=-q(1-q)\mathrm{tr}((AA^{*}+A^{*}A)B^{*}B).

We need to verify

k1≤(1+q)​‖A‖(2),22​‖B‖F2\displaystyle k_{1}\leq(1+q)\|A\|_{(2),2}^{2}\|B\|_{F}^{2} (10)

and

to obtain inequality (4). We first show inequality (10). Put J1=(B​B∗+q​B∗​B)/{(1+q)​‖B‖F2}J_{1}=(BB^{*}+qB^{*}B)/\{(1+q)\|B\|_{F}^{2}\}. Then J1J_{1} is a density matrix, and we have

The last inequality holds due to q≥0q\geq 0 and |tr⁡(J1​A∗)|=|tr⁡(J1​A)||\mathrm{tr}(J_{1}A^{*})|=|\mathrm{tr}(J_{1}A)|. From (12), it suffices to show

tr⁡(J1​(A​A∗+A∗​A))−|tr⁡(J1​A)|2≤‖A‖(2),22\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}(J_{1}(AA^{*}+A^{*}A))-|\mathrm{tr}(J_{1}A)|^{2}\leq\|A\|_{(2),2}^{2} (13)

to have (10). Let us introduce some notions to prove (13). The symbol 𝒟\mathcal{D} denotes the set of all density matrices in Mn​(ℂ)M_{n}(\mathbb{C}). Notice that 𝒟\mathcal{D} is convex, bounded, and closed. =(Σj=1n​⟨𝒖1,A​𝒗j⟩​⟨𝒗j,A∗​𝒖1⟩CLOSE\displaystyle=(\Sigma_{j=1}^{n}\langle\bm{u}_{1},A\bm{v}_{j}\rangle\langle\bm{v}_{j},A^{*}\bm{u}_{1}\rangle
